one_line: Hands-on test of AI app builders on one backend-heavy prompt; Convex's Chef produced working auth, storage and database from a single prompt, while Firebase Studio, Bolt.new (with Supabase) and v0 failed or stalled.
summary: The host gives Chef by Convex (an AI app builder that the speaker assumes is a fork of open-source Bolt.new) one long prompt asking for an A/B image-voting app with login, image storage, a one-hour test duration and login-required voting. Chef generated the app, ran and fixed a failing type check, deployed to Convex in about five seconds, and the speaker reports auth, file storage, the database and voting all working without a follow-up prompt. Chef also lets users supply their own Anthropic API key, so Convex token usage is not billed, and the Convex backend is open source and self-hostable. The same prompt in Firebase Studio (preview) produced only a placeholder page, and in Bolt.new with Supabase it spent 5 to 10 minutes retrying, then failed at sign-up with a "sign up is not a function" error. v0 produced a surprise £20 charge, and its Supabase version let the user sign up but failed on test creation with a row-level-security policy violation. The speaker concludes that Chef is the strongest of the four, but this is a single-run, one-prompt comparison with no repeated trials.

key_ideas.idea: Chef by Convex builds the full stack from one prompt, including auth, file storage, database and voting, with no follow-up prompts needed, according to the speaker.
key_ideas.detail: The app is an A/B image test with login-required voting and a one-hour duration. The speaker checks sign-up, sign-in, test creation, voting and results across two users and says the backend features were all wired up.

key_ideas.idea: Deployment to Convex is near-instant, and the Convex dashboard exposes the tables, functions, logs, schedules and files the builder created.
key_ideas.detail: The deploy step took about five seconds. Auto-generated tables included auth rate limits, tests, users and votes, along with functions such as sign in and sign out.

key_ideas.idea: Convex's pitch for AI builders is that the whole backend is defined in TypeScript, and the Convex backend is open source and self-hostable, which the speaker cites as protection against vendor lock-in.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker frames this as the reason Convex is well suited to end-to-end AI app generation, since the agent can express the backend as code.

key_ideas.idea: Chef accepts the user's own Anthropic API key, so token spend goes to Anthropic and not Convex. The free Convex tier also has a usage cap.
key_ideas.detail: The key is added under Settings, in the API key section. The speaker's free-tier account showed 19M tokens used against an 18M quota at the time of the video. Paid Convex plans include more usage.

key_ideas.idea: Firebase Studio, then in preview, returned a blueprint describing the requested features but generated only a single placeholder page.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker inspected the generated files and found only the page. The speaker says there was no clear reason why.

key_ideas.idea: Bolt.new with a Supabase backend ran into repeated errors while generating, and sign-up then failed with a runtime error.
key_ideas.detail: Generation took five to ten minutes of retries. The final sign-up failed with a 'sign up is not a function' error at the form handler.

key_ideas.idea: v0 succeeded on sign-up through Supabase, but test creation failed on a row-level-security policy violation. The speaker also reports an unexpected £20 charge on v0.
key_ideas.detail: The failure shows the generated app did not configure the Supabase RLS policies needed for inserts. The speaker's conclusion is that Chef is the winner, with a caveat that Firebase is still in preview.

techniques.name: One long, feature-complete prompt, then test each feature end to end
techniques.how: Write one prompt that lists the app, the auth requirement, storage needs and specific behaviours (duration, login-required voting). Generate, deploy, then exercise sign-up, sign-in, create, vote and results with two separate user accounts. Check the backend dashboard (tables, functions, logs, schedules, file storage) to confirm the backend was actually provisioned.
techniques.when: Evaluating an AI app builder's backend capability, or checking whether a generated app actually works beyond the preview.

techniques.name: Bring your own model key to avoid builder token markup
techniques.how: In Chef, open Settings, scroll to the API key section, and paste an Anthropic API key. Generation then bills Anthropic directly, and the built-in free token allowance is no longer needed.
techniques.when: You want to use an AI app builder without paying its per-token fees, or you have an existing model account with credit.

tools: Convex (backend, dashboard, file storage, auth, durable functions)

numbers.claim: Convex deploy of the generated app took about five seconds.
Free Convex tier showed 19M tokens used against an 18M quota.
Bolt.new with Supabase took about 5 to 10 minutes of retries before producing a result.
v0 charged the speaker £20 for an integration they did not expect.

hot_takes: Chef by Convex is 'the absolute winner' and 'the next step in AI builders', based on one run per tool with a single prompt.
Firebase Studio is still in preview, but it could catch up by adding Firebase Auth, databases and deployment, so it is not out of the race.
Builders that promise 'add this in later' for backend features are 'very annoying', a complaint about the status quo rather than a measured finding.

relevance.why: A hosted app builder comparison has no bearing on the self-hosted agent proxy, memory, inference or observability work.
Not about Claude Code CLI harnessing, checkpointing or approvals.
